'''Robert Norman Clayton''' {{postnominals|FRS}} (March 20, 1930 – December 30, 2017) was a Canadian-American chemist and academic. He was the Enrico Fermi Distinguished Service Professor Emeritus of Chemistry at the [[University of Chicago]]. Clayton studied [[cosmochemistry]] and held a joint appointment in the university's geophysical sciences department. He was a member of the [[National Academy of Sciences]] and was named a fellow of several academic societies, including the [[Royal Society]].

==Biography==
Born in [[Hamilton, Ontario]], Clayton grew up in a working-class family that supported (but could not pay for) his pursuit of higher education. None of Clayton's close family members had ever attended college. His high school teachers encouraged him to apply to [[Queen's University at Kingston|Queen's University]], and he received enough scholarship funding to attend the school. Clayton said that around half of his classmates were a decade older and had served in [[World War II]]. He said that this created a serious academic environment.<ref name=":2"/> 

After graduating from Queen's University with undergraduate and master's degrees, Clayton completed a Ph.D. in 1955 at the [[California Institute of Technology]], where he was mentored by geochemist [[Samuel Epstein (geochemist)|Samuel Epstein]].  His first academic appointment was at [[Penn State University]]. In 1958, he joined the chemistry faculty at the University of Chicago, where he took over the laboratory of Nobel Prize winner [[Harold Urey]]. From 1961 to his retirement in 2001, he held joint appointments in the chemistry and geophysical sciences departments. He directed the [[Enrico Fermi Institute]] at the university from 1998 to 2001.<ref name="Special">{{cite journal|last1=Humayun|first1=Munir|last2=O'Neil|first2=James R.|title=A Special Issue dedicated to Robert N. Clayton|journal=[[Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta]]|date=September 2003|volume=67|issue=17|pages=3097–3099|doi=10.1016/S0016-7037(03)00381-8|url=https://www.researchgate.net/publication/248431724|access-date=June 4, 2016|bibcode=2003GeCoA..67.3097H}}</ref>

==Research==
Clayton worked in the field of [[cosmochemistry]] and is best known for the use of the stable [[isotopes of oxygen]] to classify meteorites.<ref name=":2">{{Cite journal|last=Clayton|first=Robert N.|date=May 2007|title=Isotopes: From Earth to the Solar System|journal=Annual Review of Earth and Planetary Sciences|language=en|volume=35|issue=1|pages=1–19|doi=10.1146/annurev.earth.35.092006.145059|issn=0084-6597|bibcode=2007AREPS..35....1C|doi-access=free}}</ref> He was aided in his research by [[Toshiko Mayeda]], who was a specialist technician familiar with the [[mass spectrometry]] equipment required. Their first joint research paper described the use of [[bromine pentafluoride]] to extract oxygen from rocks and minerals.<ref name=":3">{{Cite journal|date=1963-01-01|title=The use of bromine pentafluoride in the extraction of oxygen from oxides and silicates for isotopic analysis|journal=Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta|language=en|volume=27|issue=1|pages=43–52|doi=10.1016/0016-7037(63)90071-1|issn=0016-7037|bibcode=1963GeCoA..27...43C|last1=Clayton|first1=Robert N.|last2=Mayeda|first2=Toshiko K.}}</ref> They developed several tests that were used across the field of meteorite and lunar sample analysis.<ref name=obit>{{cite web|url=https://news.uchicago.edu/article/2018/01/11/robert-n-clayton-one-giants-cosmochemistry-1930-2017|title=Robert N. Clayton, 'one of the giants' of cosmochemistry, 1930-2017|date=11 January 2018|website=uchicago.edu|access-date=2020-08-05}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.elementsmagazine.org/archives/e14_2/e14_2_soc_MetSoc.pdf|title=In Memoriam, Bob Clayton (1930–2017)|website=Elements Magazine|access-date=2018-08-06|archive-date=2018-08-05|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20180805234018/http://www.elementsmagazine.org/archives/e14_2/e14_2_soc_MetSoc.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal|date=1976-04-01|title=A classification of meteorites based on oxygen isotopes|journal=Earth and Planetary Science Letters|language=en|volume=30|issue=1|pages=10–18|doi=10.1016/0012-821X(76)90003-0|issn=0012-821X|bibcode=1976E&PSL..30...10C|last1=Clayton|first1=Robert N.|last2=Onuma|first2=Naoki|last3=Mayeda|first3=Toshiko K.}}</ref> 

Clayton and Mayeda studied variations in the ratio of [[oxygen-17]] and [[oxygen-18]] to the most abundant isotope [[oxygen-16]], building on their surprising finding that this ratio for oxygen-17 in particular was different from that found in terrestrial rock samples.<ref>{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ghcwDwAAQBAJ&q=asteroid+toshiko+mayeda&pg=PA89|title=Asteroids: Astronomical and Geological Bodies|last=Burbine|first=Thomas H.|date=2016-12-15|publisher=Cambridge University Press|isbn=9781316867396|pages=89|language=en}}</ref> They deduced that this difference was caused by the formation temperature of the meteorite and could thus be used as an "oxygen thermometer".<ref>{{Cite journal|date=1972-02-01|title=Oxygen isotope cosmothermometer|journal=Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta|language=en|volume=36|issue=2|pages=169–188|doi=10.1016/0016-7037(72)90005-1|issn=0016-7037|bibcode=1972GeCoA..36..169O|last1=Onuma|first1=Naoki|last2=Clayton|first2=Robert N.|last3=Mayeda|first3=Toshiko K.}}</ref> They also worked on the mass spectroscopy and chemistry of the [[Allende meteorite]]<ref name=":2" /><ref>{{Cite journal|date=1977-03-01|title=Distribution of the pre-solar component in Allende and other carbonaceous chondrites|journal=Earth and Planetary Science Letters|language=en|volume=34|issue=2|pages=209–224|doi=10.1016/0012-821X(77)90005-X|issn=0012-821X|bibcode=1977E&PSL..34..209C|last1=Clayton|first1=R. N.|last2=Onuma|first2=N.|last3=Grossman|first3=L.|last4=Mayeda|first4=T. K.}}</ref> and studied the Bocaiuva meteorite, finding that the [[Eagle Station meteorite]] was formed due to impact heating.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=Malvin|first1=Daniel J.|last2=Wasson|first2=John T.|last3=Clayton|first3=Robert N.|last4=Mayeda|first4=Toshiko K.|last5=Curvello|first5=Walter Silva|title=Bocaiuva-A Silicate-Inclusion Bearing Iron Meteorite Related to the Eagle-Station Pallasites|date=1985|journal=Meteoritics|volume=20|issue=2|pages=259–273|doi=10.1111/j.1945-5100.1985.tb00864.x|bibcode=1985Metic..20..259M|issn=0026-1114}}</ref>
They also analysed approximately 300 lunar samples that had been collected during [[NASA]]s [[Apollo Program]].<ref name="Isotopes">{{cite book |doi=10.1142/9789811206290_0033 |chapter=Toshiko Mayeda and the Isotopes of Oxygen |title=Women in Their Element |year=2019 |last1=Shindell |first1=Matthew |pages=415–421 |isbn=978-981-12-0628-3|s2cid=201220619 }}</ref> In 1992, a new type of meteorite, the [[Brachinite]], was identified.<ref>{{Cite journal|last1=E.|first1=Nehru, C.|last2=M.|first2=Prinz|last3=K.|first3=Weisberg, M.|last4=M.|first4=Ebihara|last5=N.|first5=Clayton, R.|last6=K.|first6=Mayeda, T.|date=July 1992|title=Brachinites: A New Primitive Achondrite Group|journal=Meteoritics|language=en|volume=27|issue=3|pages=267|issn=0026-1114|bibcode=1992Metic..27R.267N}}</ref> Clayton and Mayeda studied the [[Achondrite]] meteorites and showed that variations in the oxygen isotope ratios within a planet are due to inhomogeneities in the [[solar nebula]].<ref>{{Cite journal|date=1996-06-01|title=Oxygen isotope studies of achondrites|journal=Geochimica et Cosmochimica Acta|language=en|volume=60|issue=11|pages=1999–2017|doi=10.1016/0016-7037(96)00074-9|issn=0016-7037|bibcode=1996GeCoA..60.1999C|last1=Clayton|first1=Robert N.|last2=Mayeda|first2=Toshiko K.}}</ref> They analysed [[Shergotty meteorite]]s, proposing that there could have been a water-rich atmosphere in the past on [[Mars]].<ref>{{Cite journal|last=Bouvier|first=A.|display-authors=etal |date=2009|title=Martian meteorite chronology and the evolution of the interior of Mars|journal=Earth and Planetary Science Letters|volume=280|issue=1–4|pages=285–295|doi=10.1016/j.epsl.2009.01.042|bibcode=2009E&PSL.280..285B}}</ref>

==Honours and awards==
In 1981, he received the [[V. M. Goldschmidt Award]] from the [[Geochemical Society]].<ref name="Goldschmidt">{{cite web|title=V.M. Goldschmidt Award|url=http://www.geochemsoc.org/awards/vmgoldschmidtaward/|publisher=[[Geochemical Society]]|access-date=June 3, 2016|archive-date=September 7, 2015|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150907031217/http://www.geochemsoc.org/awards/vmgoldschmidtaward|url-status=dead}}</ref> The next year, the [[Meteoritical Society]] awarded him its [[Leonard Medal]].<ref name="Leonard">{{cite web|title=Leonard Medalists|url=http://meteoriticalsociety.org/?page_id=64|website=meteoriticalsociety.org|publisher=[[Meteoritical Society]]|access-date=June 4, 2016|archive-date=March 5, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160305212128/http://meteoriticalsociety.org/?page_id=64|url-status=dead}}</ref>  Clayton won the [[Elliott Cresson Medal]] from the [[Franklin Institute]] in 1985.<ref name="FI">{{cite web|title=Robert N. Clayton|url=https://www.fi.edu/laureates/robert-n-clayton|website=www.fi.edu|publisher=[[Franklin Institute]]|access-date=June 4, 2016|date=2014-01-15}}</ref> He was the 1987 recipient of the [[William Bowie Medal]] from the [[American Geophysical Union]].<ref name="Eos">{{cite journal|last1=Goldsmith|first1=Julian R.|last2=Clayton|first2=Robert N.|title=1987 William Bowie Medal to Robert N. Clayton|journal=[[Eos (magazine)|Eos]]|date=1987|volume=68|issue=27|page=624|doi=10.1029/EO068i027p00624-01|bibcode=1987EOSTr..68..624G}}</ref> Clayton became a member of the National Academy of Sciences in 1996 and won the academy's [[J. Lawrence Smith Medal]] in 2009.<ref name="NAS">{{cite news|last1=Durso|first1=Thomas|title=National Academy of Sciences' Class of 1996 sets new record|url=http://www.the-scientist.com/?articles.view/articleNo/17936/title/National-Academy-of-Sciences--Class-of-1996-Sets-New-Record/|access-date=June 3, 2016|work=[[The Scientist (magazine)|The Scientist]]|date=May 27, 1996}}</ref><ref name="NAS2">{{cite web|title=J. Lawrence Smith Medal|url=http://www.nasonline.org/programs/awards/j-lawrence-smith-medal.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20111126042732/http://www.nasonline.org/programs/awards/j-lawrence-smith-medal.html|url-status=dead|archive-date=November 26, 2011|publisher=[[National Academy of Sciences]]|access-date=June 4, 2016}}</ref> Clayton has been named a fellow of the Royal Society of London (1981) and the [[Royal Society of Canada]].<ref name=Special/> He won the [[National Medal of Science]] in 2004.<ref name="NSTMF">{{cite web|title=Robert N. Clayton|url=http://www.nationalmedals.org/laureates/robert-n-clayton|publisher=National Science and Technology Medals Foundation|access-date=June 4, 2016}}</ref> In 2008, the book ''Oxygen in the Solar System'' was dedicated to Clayton.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://news.uchicago.edu/story/solar-system-book-dedicated-robert-clayton-mr-oxygen|title=Solar system book dedicated to Robert Clayton, 'Mr. Oxygen'|website=University of Chicago News|date=22 May 2008 |language=en|access-date=2018-08-05}}</ref>
 
On December 30, 2017, Clayton died his sleep at his home in Indiana from complications of [[Parkinson's disease]].<ref name=obit />
